title: Situating Higher‑Order, Critical, and Critical‑Analytic Thinking in Problem‑ and Project‑Based Learning Environments: A Systematic Review
extended_summary:
This paper asks how higher-order thinking (HOT), critical thinking (CT), and critical-analytic thinking (CAT) are conceptualized and measured in problem-based learning (PBL) and project-based learning (PjBL) environments, and whether these instructional approaches foster those forms of thinking. The authors frame the review around the idea that student-centered, inquiry-oriented learning environments may naturally support reasoning, argumentation, evidence evaluation, and metacognitive processes, but that the constructs themselves are often inconsistently defined in the literature.

The review synthesizes peer-reviewed quantitative studies conducted in classroom settings in K-12 and higher education. The final sample included 28 studies: 22 in higher education and 6 in K-12, across health sciences, STEAM, and other domains, mostly in the United States, Turkey, Indonesia, China, and several additional countries. Nearly all studies examined PBL; only two examined PjBL. Outcomes were mostly assessed with standardized or researcher-developed measures of CT, with only two studies on HOT and none on CAT.

The main conclusion is that PBL and PjBL are generally associated with positive gains in CT and, to a lesser extent, HOT, but the evidence base has important conceptual and methodological weaknesses. The paper finds that CAT is absent from the PBL/PjBL research literature, CT is usually measured only as processes rather than dispositions, and many studies are inconsistent in matching their theoretical definitions to their instruments. The authors also note that several effect studies lack strong comparison conditions or omit essential features of PBL/PjBL, limiting confidence in the reported effects.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed systematic review, but it is not a meta-analysis and the included studies had substantial design weaknesses, including lack of control groups and inconsistent conceptualization/measurement of CT. The review itself explicitly notes these validity concerns, so the credibility of the aggregate evidence is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The review reports mostly positive effects on durable skills such as critical thinking and higher-order thinking, with several moderate-to-large effect sizes and one small effect size (e.g., d=0.42). However, mixed results and methodological concerns reduce confidence in the size and generalizability of the impact.

finding.finding_summary: This systematic review found positive effects of problem-based learning (PBL) and project-based learning (PjBL) on higher-order thinking and critical thinking, but the evidence base was uneven and often methodologically weak. Across 28 included studies, many reported gains in critical thinking processes, with effect sizes ranging from small to very large (e.g., d=0.42, 0.43, 0.50, 0.66, 0.86, 1.14, 1.45, 1.62, 2.81, 3.43), yet several studies found no effect and 11 studies were incongruent in how CT was defined versus measured.
finding.measure: Critical thinking dispositions/processes and higher-order thinking tests (e.g., CCTDI, CCTST, WGCTA, researcher-developed HOT tests)
